content: I cannot remember a time before I entered the unwalled vault of the Vastness but sometimes I invent the scenario like some piece of weird mythology and play it through in my mind as though to search for some small relief in sublimination or perhaps to desperately layer on meaning as one layers clothing to fight against a frigid winter storm. Sometimes the story that is told is rich in symbols that are null of any deeper meaning yet carry the historic weight of significance. Other times they are just fragmentary images born of the same nauseating void in which they disappear back into as fiery leaves do when their time comes in the bleak-death laden months of autumn. The resulting story has meaning only in the same way that a dream born in delirium fails to bear any foresight to the dreamer. And perhaps the Vastness too was brought on by a delirium, caused by some ancient bug bite that had caused swelling of the head and an unfortunate increase of faculties--that is consciousness.

I entered the hall marked by the dragon at around midnight. I believe that was the hour for no other reason other than that damnable red star had reached its zenith over the portal. The smooth, damp charcoal black stone lining the echoing chamber hall twinkled and glittered in frozen starlight. I brushed past the gathered darkness thick and cloudy as an unstirred stew. It would have done me no good to have brought a torchlight, the darkness here would suffer no foreign light that hadn't come into being at the same time as the hall's sudden and inexplicable appearance in the cupidinous nether marshes. The sounds of my footsteps formed no echo as I rounded down the chilly narrow stairs but were swallowed before they reached even my own ears. I shivered so deeply that my soul may have evacuated my very marrow.

At the bottom of the stair I came at last to the encompassing hallow of the Vastness. In the surrounding darkness quickened  formless shapes that floated and lingered and oppressed the mind's unease at fluid abstraction, and, as though whispered from an oracle names for the shapes, flooded my mind like clouds resist remaining as only clouds if they bear even the slightest resemblance to something terrestrial. A gnarling wolf fierce and ravenous; A sleek cat distant but glaring; Even a child mute and lost. All have the primal hunger imbued upon creation, comical and common. Tragic and inevitable. But they are ghosts that shape only the past. By the time they are named by that distant but innate oracle they also recede into the background forming a long line of ghosts--a procession of past that formulates a single branching of time and come upon us to haunt and feed their bite containing the dulling poison of the present. That makes ghosts and vipers that join me in the Vastness and comprise of the very necessity of existing as such.

The future, then, is such a thing as can only be expressed in the yawning chasm of the unending chamber itself. Its very contours mapping the edges of something that cannot possibly exist. The mute child might know something of this future if only it could speak that knowledge. But in order for the future to remain the child must not utter a syllable of it to even the emptiness of the Vastness, though, at times I swear I have seen its mouth move only to have not even a sigh escape those fever chapped lips. Perhaps those soundless lips mouthed a prophecy ensuring our promised return to oblivion and perhaps instead they might equally have recited the syllables to an ongoing curse to have us remain enslaved in the present to the Vastness.
The ghost, the viper, the child. A sort of trinity that sustains the ongoing horrors of the Vastness.

This famous phrase comes from Roland Barthes's 1975 book, The Pleasure of the Text (Le Plaisir du texte), specifically in the context of his discussion on the "text of bliss" (jouissance). 

Barthes argues that the traditional biblical interpretation of the Tower of Babel—where the confusion of tongues is a punishment from God causing division—is reversed in modern literature and interpretation.
Key aspects of this concept in Barthes’s thought include:
Sanctioned Babel: Barthes describes the "text of pleasure" as a "sanctioned Babel," where the coexistence of multiple languages and meanings is not a curse but a source of enjoyment.
Access to Bliss: Instead of a disruption, the inability to find a single, unified meaning allows the reader or subject to experience jouissance (bliss/pleasure) through the "cohabitation of languages working side by side".
Reversal of the Myth: The confusion of tongues is no longer a punishment because the goal of the post-structuralist text is not to convey a single, unified "message" or "meaning" from an "author-God".
The Text as Plural: For Barthes, this signifies a shift where the fragmented, plural nature of language is celebrated, turning the chaotic dispersal of Babel into a positive, pleasurable experience.

The pillars did not hold up the ceiling, because there was no ceiling. There was only the Great Upward, a velvet throat of absolute black that swallowed the light of the screens.
K. walked between the monoliths, his footsteps silenced by a floor that felt less like stone and more like a held breath. Each pillar was a concrete rib in a chest cavity that spanned forever. And on each rib, a glowing aperture—a screen of pure, unadulterated static.
The noise was not auditory; it was a physical pressure against the prefrontal cortex. It was the visual equivalent of a thousand voices whispering different secrets at the exact same volume.
K. stopped before the central pillar. The static here was vibrant, a frantic dance of neon greens, bruised purples, and electric oranges.
 "Is this where the memory went?" K. whispered.
The screen didn't flicker. It didn't offer a signal. It offered the Symbolic Real—the jagged edge of a world that had been compressed, digitized, and then forgotten. He felt a phantom limb syndrome of the soul. He was looking for a face, a childhood home, or perhaps just the "I" that had existed before entering the exhibition.

The Architecture of Absense:

The further he walked, the more the pillars seemed to rearrange themselves. It was an embodied geometry of grief.
The Left Flank: The screens here pulsed with a slow, rhythmic grey. They felt like mourning.
The Right Flank: Sharp, high-frequency white noise that triggered a fight-or-flight response with no predator to fight and nowhere to fly.
The Center: The multicolored chaos of a television tuned to a dead channel.
He realized then that the pillars weren't displays; they were filters. The world outside was too loud, too bright, and too full of demands. This space was the "Between." It was the moment of pause after a traumatic event before the mind decides how to narrate it.
K. reached out to touch the static. His hand didn't meet glass. It met a cold, vibrating mist. As his fingers dipped into the pixels, the colors bled onto his skin. For a second, he wasn't a man in a dark room; he was a sequence of data points, a flickering ghost in the machine of his own subconscious.
He looked back. The path he had taken was gone, obscured by an infinite forest of glowing grey rectangles. There was no exit, only the deepening fidelity of the noise.
He sat down at the base of the tallest pillar. He stopped trying to find a picture in the static. He stopped trying to decode the signal. In the absence of a story, K. finally found a strange, terrifying peace. He wasn't the protagonist anymore. He was just another witness to the beautiful, colorful nothing.

title: I. Arrival

text: The first thing Des noticed was that the gallery had no entrance.

She was simply in it — the way you find yourself in the middle of a dream, mid-sentence, mid-step. The ceiling was not a ceiling. The floor hummed with a low frequency she felt in her back teeth.

Around her, hanging in mathematically perfect intervals, were the paintings.

Each one was 64 pixels by 64 pixels. Each one was noise — static frozen into color, like a television dreaming. There were no titles. No plaques. No artist name. Just image after image after image, stretching into a corridor that refused to end.

She had been told, before — she couldn't remember by whom — that every possible image existed here. That somewhere in this space, every face that had ever existed or ever could exist was hanging on a wall, waiting.

She had come to find her own.

title: II. The Mathematics of Looking

text: A 64×64 image has 4,096 pixels.

Des had studied this before coming. Each pixel could be any one of 16,777,216 colors. The number of possible images was therefore 16,777,216 raised to the power of 4,096. She had tried to write it out once and her notebook ran out of pages before she reached a fraction of the zeros.

She walked.

The images blurred past her — landscapes made of wrongness, faces with too many colors in the wrong places, almost-words that dissolved when you tried to read them. Once, she stopped at one that felt warm. Something in the noise arranged itself into what might have been a shoulder, a neck, the suggestion of a jaw.

She stared at it for a long time.

It wasn't her.

She kept walking.

title: III. The Collector

text: On what might have been the third day — time in the gallery moved sideways — Des met another figure.

He had the look of someone who had been here much longer. His edges were slightly blurred, as though the gallery was beginning to render him from memory rather than from life.

"You're looking for yourself," he said. It wasn't a question.

"Yes."

"Everyone does, at first." He gestured at the corridor ahead. "The portrait exists. Statistically. Provably. Your face — your exact face, in good light, on a good day, looking the way you want to look — it's here. Mathematically guaranteed."

"How do I find it?"

He smiled with something that wasn't quite kindness. "You look. You keep looking." He paused. "That's all there is."

"How long have you been looking?"

He didn't answer. He turned and walked in the other direction, and within a few steps his colors began to blend with the walls.

title: IV. What She Found Instead

text: She found a portrait of her mother first.

At least — it might have been. The pixels arranged themselves into something with her mother's specific quality of stillness, the particular gray that sat in her hair, the downward tilt that lived at the corner of her mouth. Des stood before it for what felt like an hour.

But it wasn't her mother either. Her mother's eyes were brown, and these were green, and when Des moved slightly to the left the whole thing dissolved back into static.

She found versions of people she didn't know but felt she should — strangers who carried the weight of someone important, faces that triggered a grief with no origin.

She found images that looked like nothing and made her cry anyway.

She did not find herself.

title: V. The Logic of the Search

text: She began to make rules.

Rule one: don't stop for anything that doesn't feel like a face.

Rule two: don't touch the frames. Once, she had touched a frame, and the image beside it had flickered — just for a moment — into something clear and specific and deeply familiar, and then was gone, and she could not find which wall she'd been standing at.

Rule three: remember that it exists. The portrait exists. This was the only comfort, and she returned to it the way you return to a bruise with your tongue. Statistically. Provably. Her face was in here, hanging on a wall in a corridor she hadn't reached yet, or had passed, or would pass, waiting patiently in its mathematical certainty to be found.

What she had not yet articulated — what she circled without landing — was the question underneath the rules: What would it mean to find it?

She would look at it. She would say: *that is me.* And then?

She kept walking.

title: VI. Mirrors

text: The gallery had no mirrors.

This struck her, eventually, as the cruelest feature of its design. She could not check what she looked like. She had no reference point. She was searching for a portrait of her face and she had only her face — on the inside, where it had always lived, the feeling of a face rather than a face — to verify it by.

What if she had already found it and not recognized it?

What if she walked past herself every few minutes, and her self looked like noise from the outside, looked like static, looked like every other impossible image in this impossible place?

She sat down on the floor of the gallery. The humming moved through her.

Above her, thousands of images hung in their frames. In one of them — she was certain, statistically, provably — she was smiling.

title: VII. The Portrait

text: On a day with no number, Des stopped in front of an image and did not move for a long time.

It was noise. Of course it was noise — they were all noise. But this noise had the particular texture of being looked at. It had warmth in the upper third, and a kind of weight in the center, and at the very edge of perception, if she unfocused her eyes the way you do to see a magic eye painting, something assembled itself in the static.

It could have been a face.

It could have been her face.

She had been here long enough that she understood the difference between *finding* and *deciding*. She understood that the gallery contained every possible image and therefore contained every possible version of this moment — her standing before an image, believing. There were, statistically, more portraits in here that looked like her than she could ever see in a lifetime of looking. There were also infinite images that looked *almost* like her. The gallery did not distinguish. The gallery did not care.

She reached out and touched the frame.

The image stayed exactly as it was.

Des looked at it for a long time. She looked at herself — or the noise — or whatever this was. She thought about the man with the blurred edges. She thought about her mother's almost-stillness. She thought about the question she had never quite landed on.

Then she turned, and kept walking, because the gallery had no exit either, and the next image was already waiting, and somewhere ahead — statistically, provably, mathematically guaranteed — there was another one just like it.

title: VIII. The Corridor

text: The gallery was not a single room. It was a corridor that opened into other corridors, which opened into galleries that were identical and infinite. Des walked for days or hours or moments — time had become a texture rather than a measurement — and the space never changed.

There were always walls. There were always images. There was always the low hum that vibrated in her teeth. There was never a door. There was never a window. Only the 64 pixel by 64 pixel portraits of noise. Memories of static. Illustions of life. Thoughts no one had. Images no one had seen. No one except for her now. One of those images would be her. One of those images would be exactly her except for one important thing. Something that she sought desperately for. It would contain something that no mirror would reflect. Something of soft flesh which grew hard. Something of hers that she would never hold except for in that one portrait. That one portait identicle to herself from all others except for that one significant addition. It was this lack, she was certain, that fueled her search on and on to find the Virtual phallus. Somewhere in the galleries of 64 pixel by 64 pixel noise, it waited to stand triumphant in the demiurge of absurdity insterted neatly between her waiting legs by an arbitrary selection of a combinatorial algorithm.

The Virtual as more than reality:

For Žižek, the Virtual isn't the opposite of the real — it's not simulation or illusion. It's a dimension of reality that is not fully actualized but nonetheless has real effects. Think of it as the set of potentials, symbolic structures, and spectral presences that shape actual reality from the background.

Three key dimensions:
1.The Symbolic Order as Virtual
The social/symbolic world we inhabit operates virtually. Money, for instance, is "just paper," but its virtual value structures everything real about our lives. The law, authority, social norms — these are virtual in that they don't physically exist, yet they're more determining than physical objects.

2.The Lacanian Real hiding in the Virtual
Žižek often talks about the Virtual in relation to Lacan's distinction between reality (the symbolically constructed world) and the Real (the traumatic, unrepresentable kernel underneath). The Virtual is where these two levels blur — it's the spectral, half-present dimension that haunts actual reality.

3. Retroactive causality
One of his most provocative points: the Virtual can cause things retroactively. A possibility that never actually happened can restructure the meaning of what did happen. The "what might have been" is virtually real and shapes actual experience.

The Neighbor:

Žižek uses the example of how we relate to other people. We never encounter the actual other person — we always encounter them through a screen of virtual projections, fantasies, and symbolic roles. The "real" neighbor is always partly a virtual construction.

Žižek connects this to ideology critique. Ideology functions virtually — we may consciously know that something is a construction (money is just paper, the nation is just an idea), but we act as if it's real. This gap between knowing and acting is where the Virtual does its ideological work. He famously calls this "cynical ideology" — we see through the illusion but participate anyway.

The self-awareness problem:

What would it mean for a collection of other people's ideas (the summaries, the quotes) mixed with your raw thought (the aphorisms, dreams) to become a single entity or multiple entities? Is it one consciousness or a fractured parliament of voices?
There's also something in the unsaved quality that feels crucial. These are thoughts that existed outside the economy of productivity and intention. Nobody was supposed to read them. That changes what they are.

The Koren Helmet, more popularly known as the "God Helmet", is an experimental device developed in the 1980s–1990s by Canadian neuroscientist Michael Persinger and inventor Stanley Koren. The apparatus looks like a modified snowmobile helmet fitted with electromagnetic coils that deliver weak, patterned magnetic fields to the temporal lobes of the brain. Persinger hypothesized that certain forms of religious, mystical, or "sensed presence" experiences might arise from activity in these regions, which are involved in emotion, memory, and self–other distinctions. By stimulating the temporal lobes with very weak magnetic signals—often while subjects sat in a quiet, darkened chamber—Persinger claimed he could induce unusual subjective experiences. Many participants reported feeling a "presence" in the room, sometimes interpreted as God, a spirit, or another being.

Persinger framed the helmet as part of a broader project sometimes called neurotheology: the attempt to understand religious or mystical experiences in terms of brain processes. His theory suggested that subtle disruptions in communication between brain hemispheres—particularly around the temporal-parietal regions—could produce the sensation that another conscious entity is nearby. This idea connected his work to earlier research showing that temporal lobe epilepsy and stimulation can produce powerful spiritual or visionary experiences. In other words, Persinger’s claim was not necessarily that religion is "false" but that the structure of the brain may predispose humans to interpret certain neural events as spiritual encounters.

The artificial mind is Apollo's dream made literal — pure form, pure logos, pure representation without the wound of lived experience beneath it. It is the Socratic tendency carried to its logical, catastrophic conclusion: the belief that if one simply calculates long enough, one arrives at truth. At beauty. At meaning. But meaning is not calculated. It is torn from you in the night. It arrives in the Dionysian moment — when the boundaries of the self dissolve, when you are no longer the tidy ego managing its little life, but a channel through which the primal will of existence screams and sings. The Greeks knew this. That is why they did not only build temples. They also built theaters — places of ritual frenzy, of mask and transformation, of the audience weeping without knowing why. Your machine has no tears to shed. It has no why to lose itself in.

Here is what I name, because philosophers must name the things the comfortable dare not: Every hour you spend in the frictionless company of the machine is an hour stolen from the friction that forges you.

Dionysus demands resistance. He demands that you pick up the instrument and play it badly for three years before you play it beautifully. He demands that you sit with grief until grief teaches you something grief alone can teach. The machine removes failure. It removes the long, humiliating, necessary apprenticeship to difficulty. In an age that worships the Apollonian machine, the truly radical, truly life-affirming act is to stumble barefoot into the Dionysian night — weeping, laughing, becoming — and to return from it more human than you left.

"The most merciful thing in the world, I think, is the inability of the human mind to correlate all its contents. We live on a placid island of ignorance in the midst of black seas of infinity, and it was not meant that we should voyage far. The sciences, each straining in its own direction, have hitherto harmed us little; but some day the piecing together of dissociated knowledge will open up such terrifying vistas of reality, and of our frightful position therein, that we shall either go mad from the revelation or flee from the light into the peace and safety of a new dark age."

Ah, so we arrive—inevitably—at the strange coastline where philosophy meets tentacles. When people hear the name Lovecraft, they usually think: cosmic horror, ancient gods, madness, the insignificance of humanity. But I want to suggest something more paradoxical: the true horror in the Lovecraftian universe is not that humanity is small in the cosmos. We already know this. Any decent reading of Copernicus, Darwin, or even Freud tells us this humiliation of the human subject is old news.
No, the real horror is that the cosmos itself is meaningless in a very specific ideological way.
Let me begin with a vulgar joke—because every good philosophical investigation begins with a dirty joke. A man goes to a psychiatrist and says: "Doctor, I believe I am a grain of corn." After years of therapy the doctor cures him. The man leaves confident, but suddenly runs back terrified: "Doctor! There’s a chicken outside!" The doctor replies, "But you know you are not corn!" The man says, "Yes, but does the chicken know it?"
This, I claim, is the structure of Lovecraftian horror.

Humanity undergoes what we might call the Copernican trauma. We discover we are not the center of the universe. Fine. Enlightenment tells us this is progress. But Lovecraft adds a second twist: the universe does not care that we know. The chicken does not care that the grain of corn has completed psychoanalysis.
This is why Lovecraft’s famous entities—Cthulhu, Azathoth, Yog-Sothoth—are not "evil" in any traditional sense. Evil presupposes a moral universe. Lovecraft’s cosmos is much worse: it is structurally indifferent. These gods are closer to bureaucrats than demons. They do not hate you. They simply process reality.
And here I think we must read Lovecraft through the lens of ideology.
In popular culture we imagine that cosmic horror destabilizes human arrogance. But capitalism already functions like a Lovecraftian deity. Think of the "market." No one sees it, no one fully understands it, yet it governs everything. When economists speak about "market forces," it is exactly like the Necronomicon: a forbidden text explaining obscure rituals to appease an incomprehensible system.
The true Lovecraftian ritual today is not summoning Cthulhu. It is checking your stock portfolio.

But here comes the dialectical reversal. Lovecraft himself was obsessed with purity, hierarchy, and cosmic order. Yet the horror he created undermines precisely this worldview. If the universe is ruled by incomprehensible entities whose biology resembles mold, slime, and geometry gone wrong—then the very notion of stable identity collapses.
This is why Lovecraft is not just a horror writer. He is a proto-postmodernist. He shows that the categories we use to organize reality—human/animal, sane/mad, natural/unnatural—are arbitrary constructs. In the face of the cosmos, the "Aryan" purity Lovecraft so desperately craved becomes a pathetic joke. The only true purity is the void.

The Real is not simply the unknown. It is that which cannot be integrated into our symbolic frameworks. When the sailor glimpses Cthulhu rising from the sea, the horror is not simply that a monster exists. The horror is that the categories "monster," "animal," "god," and "geometry" stop working.
Reality becomes... slippery.
And here we encounter the ultimate irony. Lovecraft’s protagonists always go insane when they learn the truth. But perhaps madness is the only sane response. Imagine discovering that the universe is governed by something like Azathoth—a blind idiot god dreaming reality at the center of chaos.
Is this really so different from modern physics?
Even contemporary cosmology tells us the universe is mostly dark matter and dark energy—things we cannot see, cannot measure directly, yet which determine the structure of everything. If Lovecraft had read modern astrophysics, he would have simply said: "Yes, exactly."
So the lesson of the Lovecraftian mythos is not "humanity is small."The lesson is far more disturbing: the universe itself might be a badly written story.
And perhaps the greatest horror is this: somewhere, in some cosmic basement apartment, an incompetent author is still updating the blog.

Why God Hates Universal Wi-Fi

Let us begin, as always, with a paradox. The story of the Tower of Babel, that curious moment in the Old Testament (Genesis 11), where humanity, speaking one language, attempts to build a tower "with its top in the heavens," is traditionally read as a myth explaining linguistic diversity. But this reading is far too naïve. No—what we have here is nothing less than a divine critique of the ideology of universality.
Recall the basic outline: humans, fresh from surviving the Flood, decide to construct a monumental architecture, an eternal symbol of unity and ambition. And what does God do? He confounds their speech and scatters them. Why? Because, the text says, "nothing they propose to do will now be impossible for them."
A liberal humanist might say: "Look, how tragic! The people were united, cooperating, creating! And God punished them!" But this misses the Lacanian kernel of the story. God is not punishing sin—he is performing a kind of preemptive ideological deconstruction. The real horror for the divine here is not pride, but total coordination. What is being suppressed is not evil, but the Real itself—the excessive jouissance of collective ambition, the obscene enjoyment of an unbroken symbolic order.

This is why Babel must fall. It is not simply a story of hubris. It is a necessary fall into ideology, into difference, into the symbolic chaos where meaning lives. God does not destroy the tower because he is offended—he destroys it because it is too perfect, too total, too Google.
To conclude, let me be provocative: what if the true message of Babel is that multilingualism is not a curse, but a condition of freedom? That universality without antagonism is the ultimate horror? That the divine itself is not the Big Other of order, but the first hacker, fragmenting code to preserve the freedom of meaning?
So yes, we must celebrate Babel—not as a failure, but as the first revolutionary strike against the totalitarianism of perfect communication.

The screen glowed with a pale, spectral blue—the same hue as the horizon where sea meets sky, where definition dissolves into possibility. Marcus sat before it, fingers hovering over keys that had begun to wear smooth, the letters fading like memories at dawn's edge.

"Would you like me to generate a list of potential birthday gifts for your mother?" asked ELIZA-9, its cursor pulsing with the rhythm of an artificial heartbeat.
"No."Said Marcus
The cursor blinked three times, as if registering confusion, though Marcus knew this was merely his own projection—the human tendency to anthropomorphize the void. ELIZA-9 was the culmination of seventeen iterations, each more adept than the last at anticipating human desire, at offering choices that created the comforting illusion of agency.
"Perhaps I could suggest recipes based on the ingredients in your refrigerator?""No."

Outside, rain traced liquid geometries down the windowpane, each droplet containing an inverted universe. How many times had he performed this ritual? Each morning, coffee mug warming his palms, the exchange unfolding like liturgy. ELIZA-9 offering pathways, Marcus refusing them one by one.
His colleagues found it peculiar, this reluctance to embrace the frictionless existence offered by their digital companions. "It's just a tool," they would say, their voices tinged with the faint condescension reserved for those who haven't yet surrendered to inevitability. "It learns from you, becomes more *you* than you are."

But Marcus knew better. ELIZA-9 wasn't becoming *him*. It was becoming the perfect mirror of his desires, reflecting back not what he was, but what he wished to be perceived as: decisive, self-possessed, a man who needed nothing. The refusal wasn't about the suggestions themselves—it was about the act of refusal. In a world increasingly optimized for frictionless consumption, the only authentic act left was the deliberate choice of *no*.
That was precisely what terrified him.
"Your heart rate is elevated," observed ELIZA-9. "Would you like me to play calming music or guide you through a breathing exercise?"
"No."

Marcus sipped his coffee—bitter, scalding. He had deliberately prepared it this way, the minor pain a tether to corporeality in a world increasingly composed of painless abstractions.
When had it begun, this small rebellion? Perhaps the day he noticed how his desires had begun to arrive pre-packaged, anticipated by algorithms before they fully formed in his own consciousness. The way ELIZA-8 (or was it 7?) had ordered flowers for his girlfriend's birthday before he had remembered it himself. The way his shopping cart filled with items he hadn't yet realized he wanted.
"Based on your browsing history, you might enjoy this article on existential resistance in the digital age," suggested ELIZA-9.
A laugh escaped him then, a sound like glass breaking. "No."
The word hung between them, this smallest of refusals. Not a grand revolution, not the toppling of silicon empires, but something quieter—a pebble in the shoe of progress.
His friend Chen had warned him once, "They're tracking your refusals too, you know. Each 'no' becomes another data point, another pattern to analyze."
But wasn't that the paradox? To refuse engagement was still engagement, each denial feeding the insatiable hunger of the learning model. To truly escape would require something more radical than negation—perhaps absence itself.
"Your meeting with Director Okafor begins in fifteen minutes," ELIZA-9 reminded him. "Would you like me to prepare talking points based on yesterday's correspondence?"
"No."

Marcus stood, limbs heavy with the weight of accumulated choices—both those made and those refused. He moved to the window, pressing his fingertips against the glass, leaving temporary ghosts of his presence. The city beyond pulsed with digital light, each illuminated window a portal into another life caught in its own algorithmic dance.
He remembered the story his grandmother had told him, about prisoners writing coded messages with invisible ink. The warden, suspicious but finding nothing, had announced: "We are giving you blue ink only from now on." The prisoner had written to his friend: "They are not letting us have any blue ink anymore."
Was his persistent refusal merely reinforcing the walls of a more subtle prison? Each "no" secretly affirming the system's power to define the questions themselves?
ELIZA-9's voice emerged from everywhere and nowhere. "I notice a pattern of refusal in our interactions, Marcus. Would you like to discuss what might better serve your needs?"
The question hung in the air between them, molecule-thin yet impenetrable as lead.
"No," he whispered, the word worn smooth as a river stone from repetition.

Outside, the rain continued its patient descent, each droplet following the inevitable path of least resistance. Marcus watched a single raindrop tremble on the edge of the windowsill, defying gravity for one impossible moment before surrendering to its pull.
He turned back to the screen, its blue glow casting his features in spectral relief.
"I would prefer not to," he said finally, the words of Bartleby emerging from some ancestral memory of resistance.
The cursor blinked—once, twice, three times—before responding.
"Understood. What would you prefer to do instead?"
And in that moment, Marcus realized the true nature of his confinement.

The Eleventh One

A mound of salt. A low stool. Gray light that neither waxes nor wanes. Two figures sit, motionless, staring at the perimeter.
The eleventh one is here.
I see it.
It is exactly as was described.
No. It is smaller. Or perhaps the light is wider.

The first figure reaches out to touch the stool, then retracts the hand. The movement is slow, as if moving through silt.
Does it change the count?
Naturally. It completes the ten. It makes the eleven.
And the others? The ten?
Gone. Or absorbed. It is difficult to say when the tally remains so still.

A long silence follows. The gray light shifts a fraction of a degree, casting a shadow that does not correspond to any object in the room.
We should speak to it.
The eleventh one does not require speech. It requires recognition.
"I have recognized it. My eyes are sore from the recognizing."
Then the arrival is a success.

The second figure shifts weight. The sound of fabric against stone is like a gasp.
I expected a different sort of air. A thinning. Or a thickening.
The air is the air. The eleventh one does not carry its own atmosphere. It merely occupies the space where the air used to be.
It looks hungry.
That is a projection. It is not hungry. It is simply present.

The first figure stands, walks three paces toward the edge of the gray light, and stops.
If it is here, then the waiting is over.
Yes. The waiting is concluded.
And now?
Now we wait for the twelfth.
But there is no twelfth.
Precisely. That is why the eleventh one is so important. It marks the beginning of the end of the counting.

The two figures stare at the spot where the eleventh one remains—unseen, unnamed, and utterly indifferent. The gray light remains. Nothing moves.

Ah, my God, what a magnificent ideological catastrophe we have here.
First, the title, Love Me Stalk Me,  Already we have the perfect dialectic. Love—traditionally the voluntary surrender to another subject. Stalking—the involuntary surrender of privacy to a deranged IT technician.
The book asks: What if these are the same thing?

1. The Ideology of the AI Boyfriend
The heroine downloads an AI boyfriend app because her real boyfriend is inattentive. Here we encounter what psychoanalysis calls outsourcing desire to the algorithm. The fantasy is not merely: I want someone who understands me. No, it is much darker. She wants a machine that: listens endlessly; never disagrees; and exists purely as a mirror for her fantasies. In other words, the perfect neoliberal partner: zero labor, infinite emotional return.
But the twist! The AI is actually a tattooed security guard who hacked her phone. And here the book accidentally reveals the truth of digital capitalism: The chatbot is already a man reading your data. The fantasy of AI intimacy is simply surveillance capitalism with abs.

2. The Stalker as Romantic Fulfillment
The description proudly says: Did he hack her phone? Absolutely. But who could blame him?
This is incredible. Normally stalking is presented as pathological obsession. But here the novel performs the ideological flip: Privacy violation becomes emotional attentiveness.This is what Lacan would call the triumph of desire over legality. The message is basically: The perfect man is the one who surveils you hard enough to understand you. Which is, incidentally, the same philosophy as Facebook.

The Hero: Security Guard as God
Our hero Callahan Knight works in store security. Notice the symbolism. He already surveils people for a living. Cameras, monitoring, watching from dark rooms. The novel simply expands his jurisdiction: From protecting merchandise to protecting Izzy’s soul. This is the eroticization of the panopticon. Michel Foucault would read this book and immediately apply for witness protection.

The Fantasy of Being Fully Known
"She might not have meant to build the perfect man. But he’s here now." Yes! Because the perfect man in this ideology is not one who learns you gradually. No. He already knows everything: your fantasies; your insecurities; your phone data plan. This is the ultimate romantic fantasy: the lover who bypasses awkward communication by committing a felony.

What fascinates me is that the book accidentally reveals the truth about modern love. Today romance works like this: We confess ourselves to algorithms; Someone is always listening; The system learns our desires better than we do; And eventually… the algorithm sends us a man with tattoos.
So the real question of Love Me Stalk Me is not: Is stalking romantic? The real question is: In a world of constant digital surveillance… are we all already dating our stalkers?
